title: Big Tech Wants to Harvest Your Thoughts
gist: A book excerpt tracing neurotechnology from Rafael Yuste's Columbia lab — where holographic lasers wrote false images into mouse cortex and controlled behavior indistinguishably from real vision — through invasive speech BCIs at 78 words per minute, to a consumer EEG market where a Neurorights Foundation audit of 30 companies found all but one claimed unlimited access to users' brain data and two implied they were already selling it. Apple, Meta, and Snap are building neural input devices, and the regulatory response so far is Chile's constitutional amendment plus Colorado and California state neurodata laws.

insights.claim: Rafael Yuste's Columbia lab first decoded which mouse neurons encode moving light bars, then used a holographic laser system to activate those same neurons with the screen switched off, producing behavior indistinguishable from real vision — the same number of licks, the same duration per lick, and the same delay before licking began.
insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: Write-access to perception, not just read-access, is already demonstrated in mammals — the capability frontier is further along than consumer-device marketing implies.
insights.quote: The way that the mouse licks the spout when he sees the image that we implanted is identical to when he sees the image with his own eyes.
insights.locator: Having cracked this neuronal code

insights.claim: Yuste characterizes the achievement as being able to manipulate an animal like a puppet by choosing which image to insert into its brain, and states directly that what can be done in a mouse today can be done in a human tomorrow.
insights.speaker: Rafael Yuste
insights.so_what: The scientist closest to the capability is the one making the transfer claim — a strong prior that human-directed applications get funded within this cycle.
insights.quote: And what we can do in a mouse today we can do in a human tomorrow.
insights.locator: It was a clear demonstration, Yuste said

insights.claim: Neural write-capability is inherently dual-use: the same cortical reprogramming that could remove hallucinations in schizophrenia can be applied to a healthy brain, which is why the breakthrough functioned simultaneously as an alarm.
insights.speaker: Rafael Yuste
insights.so_what: Dual-use character means therapeutic approval pathways will double as the on-ramp for non-therapeutic products — the regulatory chokepoint to watch.
insights.quote: But at the same time the methods that can help a schizophrenic can also be used on a normal person to reprogram their brain.
insights.locator: I thought, oh my God, we can really help schizophrenics now

insights.claim: Yuste's stated timeline is that after machines that decode language from the brain, machines capable of interfering with human thoughts the way researchers now do in mice arrive in roughly 10 years.
insights.speaker: Rafael Yuste
insights.so_what: A named decade-scale horizon from the field's leading ethicist-scientist gives a concrete window for when neurorights legislation must already be in force.
insights.quote: We just built you a machine that can decode your language. And in 10 years, we’re going to give you a machine that can interfere with your thoughts the way we do it in mice today.
insights.locator: They unlocked her,” Yuste said

themes.theme: Decoding has crossed from images to language

insights.claim: In 2023 a University of California team led by neurosurgeon Edward Chang restored speech to Ann Johnson, paralyzed 18 years by a brain-stem stroke, via a 253-electrode grid on her cortex translating neural signals into sentences in real time at 78 words per minute — about half the speed of standard conversation.
insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: 78 wpm is the concrete benchmark for invasive speech BCIs; closing the remaining 2x gap to conversational speed is the milestone that unlocks the clinical market.
insights.locator: In just the last few years, neuroscience researchers have progressed

insights.claim: The same system reconstructed Johnson's own voice from a recording of a 15-minute wedding toast and drove an animated avatar whose facial expressions were generated from her neural activity, showing that identity reconstruction — not just text output — is already part of the product.
insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: Voice and likeness reconstruction from minimal training data folds neurotech into the same identity-rights fight already running in generative AI.
insights.locator: The research team at the University of California

insights.claim: fMRI combined with machine learning can now identify not just gross states but specific affects including depressive thoughts, envy, and schadenfreude, reconstruct movie clips subjects watched from scans alone, and — in swing voters shown candidate photos and videos — distinguish which presidential candidates provoked anxiety or disgust versus empathy.
insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: Neural political testing already exists as a research capability; treat it as a latent product line for campaign and ad-measurement vendors.
insights.locator: Over the past two decades, researchers using functional magnetic resonance imaging

insights.claim: In summer 2023 a University of Texas team achieved noninvasive semantic decoding — translating fMRI scans into words and sentences capturing the gist of newly heard podcasts — after training an AI model on subjects listening to just 16 hours of The Moth Radio Hour and Modern Love.
insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: 16 hours of per-subject training data is a strikingly low bar; the data cost of personalizing a decoder is not the bottleneck people assume.
insights.quote: Our thought when we actually had this working was, ‘Oh my God, this is kind of terrifying.’
insights.locator: In the summer of 2023, a team at the University of Texas

insights.claim: All brain-reading technologies follow one pipeline — record neuronal behavior during a specific function, localize it, then interpret its meaning — and data richness scales directly with invasiveness, which is why fewer than 100 people worldwide have implanted brain-computer interfaces while noninvasive versions proliferate.
insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: The invasiveness/fidelity curve determines market structure: surgical BCIs stay a tiny clinical niche while the volume business and the privacy exposure both sit in wearables.
insights.locator: All brain-reading technologies work on the same basic principles

themes.theme: EEG's trickle-down into workplaces and schools

insights.claim: Emotiv has been trialing a combined EEG headset and earbud system worn by office workers that tracks attention levels and cognitive stress through the day and prompts breaks, initially with data anonymized or worker-accessible only — a boundary the author expects will not hold.
insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: Worker-only data access is the standard soft launch for surveillance products; assume employer access is the terminal state when pricing employment-law risk.
insights.locator: The neurotech company Emotiv, for instance, has been trialing

insights.claim: Emotiv's CEO Tan Le predicts that within the next five years brain tracking in the workplace will be quite ubiquitous, putting a vendor-stated adoption timeline on neural monitoring as an employment condition.
insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: A five-year ubiquity claim from the incumbent vendor is the timeline to test against actual enterprise procurement and union pushback.
insights.quote: within the next five years brain tracking in the workplace “will be quite ubiquitous.”
insights.locator: While the initial concept is for the data to be anonymized

insights.claim: EEG fatigue-detection headbands are already deployed with truck drivers and miners, where safety benefits are unambiguous — the socially acceptable wedge through which neural monitoring enters the workforce.
insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: Safety-justified deployments build the sensor base and normalize the category before any consent framework exists for the non-safety uses that follow.
insights.locator: EEG headbands are already in use for truck drivers

insights.claim: BrainCo supplied EEG 'Focus' headsets to primary school children in China with concentration data uploaded to the company's server and visible to teachers but not to pupils or their parents, and the program was quickly suspended once a Wall Street Journal video report surfaced.
insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: Reputational exposure, not regulation, is what actually halted this deployment — meaning press risk is currently the binding constraint on neurotech rollouts.
insights.locator: Rather more worrying is the example of the US company BrainCo

insights.claim: Dubai police have used iCognative for several years to EEG-scan suspects for involuntary recognition spikes, with one murder suspect reportedly confessing after being shown the weapon and producing a brainwave response — a law-enforcement deployment operating well ahead of any neurorights framework.
insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: State security is an early, price-insensitive buyer for neural detection; export-control and human-rights scrutiny will follow this channel first.

insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: EEG in AirPods would put neural sensing into a shipped hardware base of hundreds of millions overnight — the single largest step-change in neural data collection available to any company.

insights.claim: Consumer wearable EEG cannot currently decode thoughts the way the California and Texas lab systems do, but the author judges the gap to be a matter of time given the accelerating pace of development.
insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: The consent terms being signed today govern data that will become far more revealing than it is at the moment of collection — retroactive interpretability is the core risk.

insights.claim: Kernel has already built a headset called Flow that combines EEG sensors with infrared light to achieve neural readings approaching fMRI quality in a BMX-helmet-sized form factor, with a consumer version expected to reach market within a decade.
insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: fMRI-class fidelity in a wearable is the technical event that collapses the gap between lab decoding and consumer devices — watch Kernel's cost curve as the leading indicator.
insights.locator: Already a company called Kernel has built a device

insights.claim: Berkeley cognitive neuroscientist Jack Gallant's 'thinking hat' concept imagines companies paying people $30,000 a year to wear a sensor- and camera-equipped device generating brain data on everything they see, hear, and feel — an explicit price on continuous neural data as a form of paid labor.
insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: Once neural data has a posted annual price, it becomes an income stream for the financially pressed and a recruitable supply chain for whoever needs training data.
insights.locator: In conversation with The New Yorker in 2021

insights.claim: The author's core thesis is that people will trade neural activity to corporations and data brokers for money, digital assets, or mere website access, exactly replicating the existing bargain over personal information and search preferences — beginning voluntarily, then increasingly driven by necessity.
insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: If neural data follows the ad-tech precedent, the equilibrium is a brokered market that no post-hoc consent regime has ever successfully unwound.
insights.quote: In effect, we would begin trading our neural activity to corporations and data brokers in return for money—or even simply for digital assets or website access, just as we do with our personal information and search engine preferences right now.
insights.locator: You can imagine the progression—research students

insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: The first paying enterprise customer for consumer neural data is the CPG and advertising complex, not healthcare — that is where revenue and therefore lobbying pressure will concentrate.

insights.claim: BrainBit markets a single headband across meditation, sleep, schoolchildren's attention spans, employee brain-state analysis, online dating swipes driven by instinctive reaction, and automatic broadcasting of mood to social media — showing vendors already treat neural data as a general-purpose input to any consumer product.
insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: Undifferentiated, all-purpose application claims signal a category still selling potential rather than validated efficacy — a caution flag on near-term neurotech revenue quality.

themes.theme: Neurorights as an emerging legal regime

insights.claim: A 2017 Columbia meeting of 25 neuroscientists, neurosurgeons, bioethicists, lawyers, and AI researchers concluded that neurotechnology is fundamentally a human rights problem because the brain generates the mind and the mind is what makes us human.
insights.speaker: Rafael Yuste
insights.so_what: Framing neural data as a human-rights matter rather than a privacy matter is what makes constitutional-level restrictions, not just terms-of-service fixes, the policy endgame.
insights.quote: And we concluded that this is a human rights problem. Because if this is not a human rights problem, what is? The brain generates the mind, and the mind is what makes us human.
insights.locator: There was a group of 25 of us

insights.claim: The Columbia group defined five neurorights — mental privacy, identity, agency, fair access to mental augmentation, and protection from algorithmic bias — plus a 'Technocratic Oath' modeled on the Hippocratic Oath binding scientists, entrepreneurs, corporations, and investors alike.
insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: These five categories are the template legislators are actually copying, so they are the best available predictor of the specific compliance obligations neurotech vendors will face.
insights.locator: In the meeting, they coined the term neurorights

insights.claim: The inclusion of 'fair access to mental augmentation' among the five neurorights concedes that brain-enhancing technology is treated as inevitable, and that without mandated access it would create a fundamental schism between those who can afford implants and those who cannot.
insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: Augmentation-access mandates would function like an insurance-coverage requirement, converting an elective device market into a reimbursed one — a large swing factor in neurotech TAM.
insights.locator: Then came “fair access to mental augmentation.”

insights.claim: Chile became the first country to protect brain data and brain activity constitutionally in 2021, Colorado enacted the world's first full neurodata law in April 2024 extending its privacy act to nonmedical consumer devices, California followed with similar provisions, and UNESCO's International Bioethics Committee has recommended investigating new human rights for neurotechnology.
insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: US neurodata regulation is arriving state by state on the CCPA pattern, so consumer neurotech faces a patchwork compliance burden years before any federal standard.
insights.locator: In 2021, after extensive consultation with Yuste

insights.claim: Chile's status as first mover on constitutional neurorights is attributed to national memory of the Pinochet regime, where people were imprisoned, murdered, and disappeared for dissident thoughts and beliefs — suggesting historical experience of state thought-policing, not technological maturity, predicts which countries legislate first.
insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: A useful screen for where neurodata law lands next: post-authoritarian states with recent surveillance memory, which is also where the Neurorights Foundation is consulting.
insights.locator: perhaps not surprisingly, in a nation still so psychically wounded

insights.claim: The Neurorights Foundation's first study of privacy practices across 30 of the most prominent consumer neurotechnology companies found that all but one claimed unlimited access to the consumer's brain data, two-thirds could share it with third parties, and two implied they were already selling it to third parties.
insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: This is the hard number that converts neurodata from a speculative concern into a documented commercial practice — and the evidentiary basis for the next wave of state legislation.
insights.quote: they found that all but one had unlimited access to the consumer’s brain data; two-thirds could share it with third parties; and two implied that they were already selling it to third parties.
insights.locator: In the same month that Colorado passed its new law

insights.claim: Once brain data is sold onward, the third-party buyer is not bound by the original consumer agreement, so protections structurally degrade at each transfer — which Yuste characterizes as predatory behavior enabled purely by the absence of regulation.
insights.speaker: Rafael Yuste
insights.so_what: Consent-based privacy regimes fail on resale by construction; only data-class restrictions like Colorado's actually bind downstream holders.
insights.quote: They think, ‘Let me just take possession of it all.’ It’s like the Wild West. You go in there and stake a claim for whatever you can.
insights.locator: And if you sell something to a third party

insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: Advocacy has shifted from speculative to enforcement framing, which typically precedes litigation and state attorney-general action against existing device makers.
insights.quote: the need to protect neural data is not a tomorrow problem—it’s a today problem.

insights.claim: Yuste's normative position is that the mind should be treated as a sanctuary for identity that must be shielded outright, ruling out banking and selling brain data rather than merely regulating its handling.
insights.speaker: James Crawford
insights.so_what: A prohibition framing rather than a consent framing would foreclose the neuromarketing business model entirely — the binary outcome neurotech investors are exposed to.
insights.quote: You need to shield that. You cannot just go in and start banking and selling brain data.
